transcript.text: We had a power cut last night and now our Candy washer dryer is completely dead - no lights, nothing. Everything else in the house came back on. The plug fuse is fine, I swapped it. Help!

A power cut can sometimes leave a specific socket dead, trip a local RCD, or blow a fuse in the spur box even if the rest of the house is fine. The next step is to confirm whether the wall socket itself has power. Please plug a different working appliance (like a lamp or phone charger) into that same socket. Does it work? If the socket works, we'll need to look inside the machine at the mains filter or PCB. If the socket doesn't work, the issue is with your home's wiring or fuse box.
Yes, I tried a lamp in that socket and it works fine. I've also left the washer-dryer unplugged for over 10 minutes and tried again, still completely dead.

Since the socket has power but the machine remains completely dead after a reset, the fault lies within the appliance's incoming power path. The most common component to fail in this scenario—especially following a power cut—is the mains interference suppressor (also called the mains filter). This is a small black block where the main power cable enters the machine; it protects the electronics from surges and can blow internally like a fuse. The next step is to check if power is actually reaching inside the casing. Please switch off and unplug the washer-dryer. Remove the top panel (usually two screws at the back) or the rear panel to access the mains entry point. Look for a small black rectangular block with wires coming in from the plug and going into the machine—this is the mains filter/interference suppressor. Check if the wires are loose, burnt, or broken at the terminals. If you can see it clearly, does it look intact and securely connected?

Sorry, I'm not comfortable taking the panels off and poking around the electrics, so I won't do that. The plug and cable look fine and there's no burnt smell from the back. Is there anything else I can check, or should I get someone in?

Since the socket is working and you are not comfortable opening the machine to check the internal components, there is nothing further you can safely do. The symptoms point to a failed internal component—most likely the mains interference suppressor that protects the electronics from power surges (which fits with the recent power cut), or potentially the control board itself. This requires an engineer to diagnose and replace the faulty part. I would recommend calling a qualified appliance repair technician.
